What if there were a way to generate long-term competitive returns without the need to endure extreme swings in volatility? This would seem to contradict CAPM and the other maxims related to risk and return. But a growing body of research indicates that, with a carefully curated portfolio, investors can indeed assume less risk and still beat the market over time by investing in low-volatility stocks. By doing so, investors can gain confidence to stay invested in equities through turbulent times. Low-volatility strategies can come in different forms.
But here’s the catch: to realize these long-term excess returns, investors would need to accept that a 90%/70% portfolio does not behave in the same way as the broader market. That’s an easy pill to swallow when the market is whipsawing the way it has this year. After all, in market downturns, this low-volatility strategy would only expose investors to 70% of the market’s downside. The real test comes during rallies, when the 90%/70% would underperform the market.
Companies like these can help low-volatility strategies limit downside capture—that is to say, exposure to falling markets—while still participating in market gains, but not fully. In the same way that climbing a hill is easier when you start halfway up, stocks that lose less in market downturns have less ground to regain when the market recovers. As a result, they’re better positioned to compound off those higher returns during subsequent rallies, resulting in better long-term performance. This concept can be illustrated by plotting a so-called 90%/70% portfolio against a global index of investment-grade stocks—in this case, the MSCI World Index (Display).

This article tests the adage and investment strategy “cut your losses and let your profits run” for randomly chosen portfolios composed of large US stocks. It is found that any cut-your-losses strategy clearly underperforms the buy-and-hold strategy. The results hold for monthly, quarterly, and annual data and even for daily data around the 2008 Financial Crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak. Cutting losses during the 2008 crisis performs better than the benchmark for half of all portfolios but not consistently and not during the 2020 crisis.
The article demonstrates that the poor performance of the adage is due to weak loser stocks (that do not strictly fall) and strong winner stocks (that do strictly rise), which implies that the best strategy is to let both losses and profits run. The results also question the relevance of the disposition effect, as we do not find any evidence that holding losers too long is bad for investors. Furthermore, it is argued that investors are lucky that “cut your losses” is not strictly implemented by all investors, as markets would frequently break down as a consequence.A graphical abstract can be found in the PDF and supplementary material for this article.

###### Abstract

Hierarchical clustering and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) mitigate the mathematical ill-conditioning of classical Markowitz covariance matrices. However, two structural vulnerabilities persist in equity markets: (1) symmetric variance penalizes upside and downside return dispersion identically, inducing acute return drag against soaring momentum sectors; and (2) unconstrained Hidden Markov Models (HMM) exhibit hyper-active regime switching (whipsaw instability), incurring excessive turnover and transaction drag. ## Abstract.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently gained popularity in stock trading for their ability to process multimodal financial data. keenable.snippet: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.

keenable.title: Active Portfolio Management in Concentrated Equity Markets
keenable.snippet:
In this paper, we develop a general and tractable stochastic control framework to address the following natural and important question: can we use information about market diversity and dispersion to exploit the benefits of diversification and volatility harvesting, while protecting the portfolio from increases in market concentration?

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to combine (i) an explicit stochastic model for the joint dynamics of market diversity and dispersion, (ii) optimization of a *time-varying* functionally generated portfolio under (quadratic) trading-cost penalties, and (iii) a stochastic optimal control formulation within SPT.

keenable.title: Interpretable Allocation and Model-Predictive Rebalancing of Equity Portfolios, Tested on Real and Synthetic Markets
keenable.snippet:
A live equity portfolio poses three problems: which stocks to hold, when to trade,
and whether the strategy holds up beyond the observed market. We built one
system for all three and tested it on 373 US equities, calibrated on 2014–2024 and
traded January 2025 to September 2026. A selection rule chose stocks by score,
by a bandit or at random, and one of seven weighting rules, four consumer-theory
utilities and three standard portfolios, set share counts under limits on budget,
single-stock weight, portfolio volatility and turnover, with each stock’s preference
weight a bounded score of its trend, market beta and the market’s recent direction.
A model-predictive controller forecast portfolio value with a multi-asset geometric
Brownian motion and re-planned at its horizon, when the value left its forecast
band, or at a drawdown stop. To probe deeper declines than the real window
held, we also ran the system on simulated markets from per-asset hidden Markov
generators with jumps, linked by market and sector factors. On real prices, the
stocks chosen mattered more to terminal wealth than the weighting rule, and the
early re-plans shrank the worst drawdown in most rule combinations against a fixed
calendar without consistently raising wealth. In the deepest simulated declines,
every combination, random picks included, ended above simulated SPY and the
equal-weight universe in the median, even without early re-plans, so the margin
came from shared parts of the system, not from stock selection or re-plan timing. A
market hedge that tightened a beta cap as the market weakened cost wealth on real
prices but paid off in the most sustained simulated declines, and the generator’s
persistent trends favored score-based selection more than the real market did, which
suggests a synthetic test judges stock selection fairly only if its generator does not
build in that persistence.

keenable.title: Are Three Matrices All You Need To Beat the Market? Observable Matrix Dynamics for Portfolio Optimization
keenable.snippet:
Abstract
We present a simple framework for dynamic portfolio management that uses nothing
but daily prices, trading volumes, and market capitalizations. Its state is three fixed-size
matrices built from the price history: the distance matrix of the return correlations and the
transition matrices of two Markov chains that rank the S&P 500 names monthly by trailing
return and by trailing volatility. These three matrices rest on the price history alone, the
same information Markowitz mean-variance optimization draws on, but they replace its
expected-return vector and covariance matrix. Our method requires no matrix inversion,
works on outlier-robust cross-sectional ranks, and is dynamic rather than single-period.
Empirically the volatility rank is forecastable one step ahead while the return rank stays
close to unforecastable. A portfolio built on the forecasts, a market-neutral momentum
long-short blended with an opportunistic long-only sleeve, beats the market on two non-
overlapping out-of-sample test sets, January 2022 to December 2024 and January 2025 to
July 2026, at Sharpes of 1.06 and 1.32 against the market’s 0.78 and 1.14, respectively, net of
a five-basis-point trading cost and marked to market daily. It also outperforms the classical
minimum-variance and maximum-diversification portfolios. Diversifying the long sleeve by
residual distance adds a further edge on both periods, lifting the Sharpe to 1.08 and 1.44
and the annualized return from 18% to 20% and from 44% to 56%, respectively. A convex
information-leader overlay separately insures the market-neutral sleeve, buying convexity
and a shallower drawdown at a small cost in return, the Sharpe unchanged.

keenable.title: Simple Portfolios that Deliver Consistent Decent Returns
keenable.snippet: Industry, on the other hand, operates under real constraints, but its data and methods are proprietary and largely unpublished. Neither is directly available to the private investor. This paper is an empirical study of established portfolio construction methods in the setting of the private investor. We consider a small investable universe of liquid US ETFs, where trading is monthly and carries a cost, and neither shorting nor leverage is permitted. Portfolio construction is posed as a convex optimization problem, its inputs are estimated from public data, and every parameter is interpretable. We denote such portfolios simple. We show that simple portfolios of as few as three ETFs deliver consistent and decent returns, without tuning to the backtest period. To find them, we have developed a framework, which we share publicly, able to backtest hundreds of portfolios on a standard laptop over a twenty year period or longer. When no return forecast is made, portfolios are constructed from risk alone, using methods such as risk parity and minimum volatility, built on a statistical factor model fitted with expectation maximization. When a forecast is made, we combine the Markowitz formulation with momentum signals and ridge regression. We report what works and what each component adds, weighing its gain against its complexity and the effort it demands of the investor. The findings are supported by numerical experiments over the past two decades, and the proposed portfolios outperform the standard 60/40 allocation.

keenable.title: RegimeFolio: A Regime Aware ML System for Sectoral Portfolio Optimization in Dynamic Markets
keenable.snippet: Financial markets are inherently non-stationary, with shifting volatility regimes that alter asset co-movements and return distributions. Standard portfolio optimization methods, typically built on stationarity or regime-agnostic assumptions, struggle to adapt to such changes. We present a simple framework for dynamic portfolio management that uses nothing
but daily prices, trading volumes, and market capitalizations. Its state is three fixed-size

and the annualized return from 18% to 20% and from 44% to 56%, respectively. A convex

Abstract
This paper evaluates the profitability of an industry-based long-only trend-following portfolio. Utilizing 48 industry portfolios from 1926 to 2024, our analysis explores the model’s profitability over a century, highlighting its adaptability and effective- ness across diverse market epochs. We assess the overall profitability of the model and examine the distribution of long-term returns and associated risks.

# Winners vs. Losers: Momentum-based Strategies with Intertemporal Choice for ESG Portfolios
###### Abstract
This paper introduces a state-dependent momentum framework that integrates ESG regime switching with tail-risk-aware reward–risk metrics.
Using a dynamic programming approach and solving a finite-horizon Bellman equation, we construct long–short momentum portfolios that adjust to changing ESG sentiment regimes.
Unlike traditional momentum strategies based on historical returns, our approach incorporates the Stable Tail Adjusted Return ratio and Rachev ratio to better capture downside risk in turbulent markets.

We find that ESG-loser portfolios significantly outperform ESG-winner portfolios in pro-ESG regimes, a counterintuitive result suggesting that market overreaction to ESG sentiment creates short-term pricing inefficiencies.

seltz.snippet:
This page walks you through backtesting the way a careful person would do it, not the way a course sells it. You will learn how to write your rules down, where to get data, what costs to subtract, and the three mistakes that make almost every backtest look better than reality.

## What is the step-by-step way to test a trading strategy on past Indian market data?

Backtesting means running your exact buy and sell rules over past NSE or BSE data to see what they would have earned. Write the rules down, pick at least ten years of data including a crash, subtract brokerage, STT and taxes, then check the worst loss you would have had to sit through.

### Key Takeaways

- A backtest is only as honest as the rules you wrote down before you looked at the chart.
- Ten years minimum, and the period must include at least one crash and one boring sideways year.
- Costs and taxes are not a footnote in India, they are often the whole difference between profit and loss.
- If your list of stocks does not include the ones that got delisted, your result is fake.
- As of August 2026, only 22.0% of the 1,518 Indian companies with full-year fundamentals clear a basic quality bar, so a strategy that assumes a large pool is already wrong.
- The number that decides whether you can actually follow the strategy is the worst fall, not the return.

## What does backtesting a trading strategy actually mean?

Backtesting is a rehearsal. You take a set of rules, you run them over market data from the past, and you see what would have happened if you had followed those rules without ever changing your mind. That last part is the whole point. In real life you skip trades, you hold losers, you double down after a bad week. A backtest strips all of that away and shows you what the rules alone produce.

It is not a prediction. Nobody can promise that what worked from 2015 to 2025 will work from 2026 onward.

ultimate.title: Mitigating Return Drag and Regime Whipsaws in Sector Rotation: An Asymmetric Downside-Aware Nested Clustered Optimization Framework
ultimate.snippet:
###### Abstract

Hierarchical clustering and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) mitigate the mathematical ill-conditioning of classical Markowitz covariance matrices. However, two structural vulnerabilities persist in equity markets: (1) symmetric variance penalizes upside and downside return dispersion identically, inducing acute return drag against soaring momentum sectors; and (2) unconstrained Hidden Markov Models (HMM) exhibit hyper-active regime switching (whipsaw instability), incurring excessive turnover and transaction drag. We propose Asymmetric Downside-Risk Nested Clustered Optimization with Sticky Regime Dynamics (Asym-Sticky-NCO) for tactical sector rotation across all 11 S&P 500 GICS sectors. The framework substitutes symmetric covariance with the Bawa-Lindenberg downside semi-covariance matrix across both hierarchical tree clustering and two-stage allocation. Furthermore, we introduce a Sticky Gaussian HMM incorporating a diagonal self-transition persistence prior ($\kappa$) and confidence-adaptive boundaries ($\delta$) to enforce macroeconomic persistence. Strictly non-anticipative walk-forward backtesting across 65 out-of-sample months (August 2020 to December 2025) demonstrates that the architecture elevates CAGR from 10.65% (Plain NCO) to 13.41% (+276 bps/year), delivers a 97.74% total return versus 72.99%, suppresses maximum drawdown to 14.22% (versus 23.93% for the S&P 500), and achieves a Calmar ratio of 0.94 (+38.2% over S&P 500; +84.3% over Baseline Regime-NCO). Crucially, sticky dynamics cut regime whipsaws by 75.0% (from 16 to 4 switches) and reduce monthly turnover from 60.78% to 30.48%, addressing core limitations of machine learning asset allocation.

ultimate.snippet:
In this paper, we develop a general and tractable stochastic control framework to address the following natural and important question: can we use information about market diversity and dispersion to exploit the benefits of diversification and volatility harvesting, while protecting the portfolio from increases in market concentration?

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to combine (i) an explicit stochastic model for the joint dynamics of market diversity and dispersion, (ii) optimization of a *time-varying* functionally generated portfolio under (quadratic) trading-cost penalties, and (iii) a stochastic optimal control formulation within SPT.

ultimate.title: Interpretable Allocation and Model-Predictive Rebalancing of Equity Portfolios, Tested on Real and Synthetic Markets
ultimate.snippet:
A live equity portfolio poses three problems: which stocks to hold, when to trade,
and whether the strategy holds up beyond the observed market. We built one
system for all three and tested it on 373 US equities, calibrated on 2014–2024 and
traded January 2025 to September 2026. A selection rule chose stocks by score,
by a bandit or at random, and one of seven weighting rules, four consumer-theory
utilities and three standard portfolios, set share counts under limits on budget,
single-stock weight, portfolio volatility and turnover, with each stock’s preference
weight a bounded score of its trend, market beta and the market’s recent direction.
A model-predictive controller forecast portfolio value with a multi-asset geometric
Brownian motion and re-planned at its horizon, when the value left its forecast
band, or at a drawdown stop. To probe deeper declines than the real window
held, we also ran the system on simulated markets from per-asset hidden Markov
generators with jumps, linked by market and sector factors. On real prices, the
stocks chosen mattered more to terminal wealth than the weighting rule, and the
early re-plans shrank the worst drawdown in most rule combinations against a fixed
calendar without consistently raising wealth. In the deepest simulated declines,
every combination, random picks included, ended above simulated SPY and the
equal-weight universe in the median, even without early re-plans, so the margin
came from shared parts of the system, not from stock selection or re-plan timing. A
market hedge that tightened a beta cap as the market weakened cost wealth on real
prices but paid off in the most sustained simulated declines, and the generator’s
persistent trends favored score-based selection more than the real market did, which
suggests a synthetic test judges stock selection fairly only if its generator does not
build in that persistence.

ultimate.title: Are Three Matrices All You Need To Beat the Market? Observable Matrix Dynamics for Portfolio Optimization
ultimate.snippet:
Abstract
We present a simple framework for dynamic portfolio management that uses nothing
but daily prices, trading volumes, and market capitalizations. Its state is three fixed-size
matrices built from the price history: the distance matrix of the return correlations and the
transition matrices of two Markov chains that rank the S&P 500 names monthly by trailing
return and by trailing volatility. These three matrices rest on the price history alone, the
same information Markowitz mean-variance optimization draws on, but they replace its
expected-return vector and covariance matrix. Our method requires no matrix inversion,
works on outlier-robust cross-sectional ranks, and is dynamic rather than single-period.
Empirically the volatility rank is forecastable one step ahead while the return rank stays
close to unforecastable. A portfolio built on the forecasts, a market-neutral momentum
long-short blended with an opportunistic long-only sleeve, beats the market on two non-
overlapping out-of-sample test sets, January 2022 to December 2024 and January 2025 to
July 2026, at Sharpes of 1.06 and 1.32 against the market’s 0.78 and 1.14, respectively, net of
a five-basis-point trading cost and marked to market daily. It also outperforms the classical
minimum-variance and maximum-diversification portfolios. Diversifying the long sleeve by
residual distance adds a further edge on both periods, lifting the Sharpe to 1.08 and 1.44
and the annualized return from 18% to 20% and from 44% to 56%, respectively. A convex
information-leader overlay separately insures the market-neutral sleeve, buying convexity
and a shallower drawdown at a small cost in return, the Sharpe unchanged.

ultimate.title: Simple Portfolios that Deliver Consistent Decent Returns
ultimate.snippet: Industry, on the other hand, operates under real constraints, but its data and methods are proprietary and largely unpublished. Neither is directly available to the private investor. This paper is an empirical study of established portfolio construction methods in the setting of the private investor. We consider a small investable universe of liquid US ETFs, where trading is monthly and carries a cost, and neither shorting nor leverage is permitted. Portfolio construction is posed as a convex optimization problem, its inputs are estimated from public data, and every parameter is interpretable. We denote such portfolios simple. We show that simple portfolios of as few as three ETFs deliver consistent and decent returns, without tuning to the backtest period. To find them, we have developed a framework, which we share publicly, able to backtest hundreds of portfolios on a standard laptop over a twenty year period or longer. When no return forecast is made, portfolios are constructed from risk alone, using methods such as risk parity and minimum volatility, built on a statistical factor model fitted with expectation maximization. When a forecast is made, we combine the Markowitz formulation with momentum signals and ridge regression. We report what works and what each component adds, weighing its gain against its complexity and the effort it demands of the investor. The findings are supported by numerical experiments over the past two decades, and the proposed portfolios outperform the standard 60/40 allocation.

ultimate.title: RegimeFolio: A Regime Aware ML System for Sectoral Portfolio Optimization in Dynamic Markets
ultimate.snippet: Financial markets are inherently non-stationary, with shifting volatility regimes that alter asset co-movements and return distributions. Standard portfolio optimization methods, typically built on stationarity or regime-agnostic assumptions, struggle to adapt to such changes. To address these challenges, we propose RegimeFolio, a novel regime-aware and sector-specialized framework that, unlike existing regime-agnostic models (e.g., DeepVol, DRL optimizers), integrates explicit volatility regime segmentation with sector-specific ensemble forecasting and adaptive mean–variance allocation. This modular architecture ensures forecasts and portfolio decisions remain aligned with current market conditions, enhancing robustness and interpretability in dynamic markets. RegimeFolio combines three components: (i) an interpretable VIX-based classifier for market regime detection; (ii) regime and sector-specific ensemble learners (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) to capture conditional return structures; and (iii) a dynamic mean–variance optimizer with shrinkage-regularized covariance estimates for regime-aware allocation. We evaluate RegimeFolio on 34 large cap U.S. equities from 2020 to 2024. The framework achieves a cumulative return of 137%, a Sharpe ratio of 1.17, a 12% lower maximum drawdown, and a 15–20% improvement in forecast accuracy compared to conventional and advanced machine learning benchmarks. These results show that explicitly modeling volatility regimes in predictive learning and portfolio allocation enhances robustness and leads to more dependable decision-making in real markets.
